utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Good morning, Mr. Vujicic. Do you hear me well in your language? I repeat. Good morning, Mr. Vujicic. Do you hear me well in your language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I'm not Vujicic. I'm Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was mistaken in the order of witnesses. Then would you kindly take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivanovic. Please make yourself comfortable. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, your Excellencies. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: JANKO IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you, Mr. Ivanovic, give a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: JANKO IVANOVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we call up 1D5591. And I hope you have a copy of your statement in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JANKO IVANOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the fifth page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see on the screen if this is your signature?

utterances.speaker: JANKO IVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we also show page 1 in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Not the first page of the document but the one before this.

utterances.speaker: JANKO IVANOVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this the page before, the first page of your statement?

utterances.speaker: JANKO IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have to make a pause between my questions and your answers, and I should like you to do the same to enable interpretation. Have you read this statement?

utterances.speaker: JANKO IVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does it accurately reflect what you've stated?

utterances.speaker: JANKO IVANOVIC
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to put the same questions to you today, would your answers be essentially the same?

utterances.speaker: JANKO IVANOVIC
utterances.text: One hundred per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to tender this package under 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Provided that the statement is redacted in accordance to your order of 21st November, 2012, there will be no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I understood that the Chamber ordered paragraphs 4 and 5 to be redacted, but I note that that hasn't been done yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll do that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you're tendering one associated exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You have no objection to the admission of that map?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: With the understanding that para-4 and 5 will be redacted, we'll admit them both. Shall we give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2763 for the statement and the associated exhibit shall be D2764. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I shall now read the summary of Mr. Ivanovic's statement in English. [In English] Janko Ivanovic spent the war in Hrasnica, Sarajevo suburb, on territory controlled by the Muslim forces. He worked as a railway employee but during the war he was forced to report to the labour detail command. He had knowledge -- I see other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honour, only this last bit that Mr. Karadzic read is redacted, as well as paragraph 4 and 5 of this anticipated summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to say for the record that I really do not see any reason why we should be so strict as to redact information that affected people's lives and behaviour. What these people has suffered has affected them and their behaviour. This is not to justify anyone --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, this is not a time for your submission.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Okay. He had knowledge that Muslim forces were using the bank in Hrasnica as their military department. He would see Muslim soldiers moving every day in the direction of Igman and military equipment frequently passed through the tunnel that connected them to the town. In April 1992, the Muslim forces attacked Krtelj Special Police forces seat and seized two armoured personnel carriers which were brought to Hrasnica and positioned near civilian building and houses. Practically every day the Muslim forces fired -- would fire cannon shells at Serbian positions and areas. And if there was return fire, it would fall near the two skyscrapers and the post office where the 4th Motorised Brigade command was located. In 1993, Janko Ivanovic had to report to labour detail command. The military police took his car in his garage. He -- they placed -- I see the Prosecutor, but I would like to -- to stress that this is the basis how this witness could have seen many things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is not a time for your question. Please be careful about what has been redacted, and then if -- in order to supplement what's -- what's in the statement, you may ask some supplementary questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: To the extent necessary and relevant. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: They placed grenades in both the glove compartment and the trunk of the car. It was returned 20 days later completely destroyed and so on --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic just continues the same thing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Janko Ivanovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, in the future, please bear in mind and pay attention to what has been ruled in the Chamber's ruling, and please try to reflect in the summary that is to be read out by Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think that's the problem is that the team didn't pick up that order and has -- have drafted a summary that didn't include the redacted portion. So Dr. Karadzic doesn't have in front of him the statement and the order such that he's able to change the summary spontaneously. So if you prefer, we could take a five-minute recess and we could sort that out and inform him of what's been redacted from the statement so that he could adjust the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zec. I remember you rose at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. In accordance -- when I'm looking at this, and this be the summary, this paragraph and the next paragraph are redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm a bit at a loss. Let's move on. I think we can move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Janko Ivanovic could not leave Hrasnica or the Muslim part of Sarajevo to cross into civilian territory. To do so, 10.000 German marks had to be paid to the Muslim authorities. He also noticed that there was no electricity in his building. However, there was in the Muslim flats in the building next to his.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, I should only like to ask you, how are you able and under what circumstances to see what was going on outside your building? On what occasions were you able to see all that was in existence in Hrasnica?

utterances.speaker: JANKO IVANOVIC
utterances.text: I was not able to see anything, because I had no electricity. The TV did not work. It's not like there was always electricity. It was available later when they switched it on from Pazaric and some people got power back, but not me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Under what circumstances were you able to move around Hrasnica, on what occasions?

utterances.speaker: JANKO IVANOVIC
utterances.text: As for Hrasnica, I was able to move around, but I did not get out except those times when I got news that somebody got killed or died, and then I went out to bury them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Whom did you bury in Hrasnica?

utterances.speaker: JANKO IVANOVIC
utterances.text: I buried Serbs who died or got killed while digging trenches on the forward line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivanovic. I have no further questions for you for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JANKO IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Zec. Before you do that. Mr. Ivanovic, do you hear me well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Your evidence in chief has been admitted in writing and now you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ivanovic. I will be asking you --

utterances.speaker: JANKO IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I will be asking you several questions about the statement that you provided. First, can you tell us was it Milomir Savcic, representative of the Karadzic Defence team, who talked to you and took the statement from you?

utterances.speaker: JANKO IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: In your statement, it's in paragraph 2, you say that you marked a map to identify several locations in Hrasnica, and the map is ID08552, which has received Exhibit D02764.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And if we could look at the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, I assume you don't speak or write English, do you?

utterances.speaker: JANKO IVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. No. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So if you look at the map, we can see titles of the locations in English. So my understanding is that you didn't actually mark this map but perhaps something else based on which this map was produced. Would it be correct?

utterances.speaker: JANKO IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Also in your statement you indicate there was a post office in Hrasnica. Would you be able to mark on this map the location of the post -- of the post office?

utterances.speaker: JANKO IVANOVIC
utterances.text: The post office was close to the two high-rises, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I understand, but would you be able to mark on the map? If not, you can say, no problem.

utterances.speaker: JANKO IVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Okay. We can move on. In paragraph 2 of the statement, you referred to Muslim soldiers. As I understand from your statement, these soldiers were living in the apartments in Hrasnica, and they were leaving their homes in order to take positions at front lines outside Hrasnica. Is this correct understanding of your statement?

utterances.speaker: JANKO IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. They did not have their own barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And they -- in fact, they were living in their apartments together with their other family members; correct?

utterances.speaker: JANKO IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Would you be able to tell us if you can remember how many families lived in Hrasnica during the war?

utterances.speaker: JANKO IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, before the war lots of them lived in Hrasnica. During the war, some fled to the Serbian side, and only about 30 per cent of the pre-war population were left, and we were all involved in the work platoon or civilian protection. I mean only men.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Okay. In paragraph 2 of your statement, you say that in April 1992, the Muslims attacked Krtelj. So when you say Krtelj, you're actually referring to a location near Ilidza where the building of the Special Police Unit of the BiH MUP was located; correct?

utterances.speaker: JANKO IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Close to Butmir. That's where the police building was even before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Okay. Let me show you an official report prepared by Tihomir Glavas who was chief of the Serb police station at Ilidza, and it talks about this event at Krtelj.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And if we can have P02308.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, you will see a report that talks about the events prior and after the establishment of the Serb police station at Ilidza. At page 2 in both languages it talks about events at Krtelj and says: "First armed action by police members was organised for April 1992 on the building of MUP special unit in Krtelj..." Then it goes on, refers to convoys of Muslims coming in. And then says: "In the armed conflict that took place on this spot, one Muslim was found, 12 armoured devices were captured, as well as big amount of other equipment." Also says that two convoys were captured near the health centre at Ilidza. So, Mr. Ivanovic, according to this report there was a conflict in Krtelj on 4 April 1992, and the Serb police members seized equipment. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: JANKO IVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I did not see it. All I know was that people said that two APCs had been brought to Hrasnica. I mean the Muslim side brought them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And these personal carriers from Krtelj were also used that -- that they were captured from Krtelj, they were also used by the Serbian Territorial Defence. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: JANKO IVANOVIC
utterances.text: I do not know about that. I did not know that, and I did not see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we call 65 ter 32786.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, you're going to see now transcript of the intercept telephone conversation between Miroslav Gagovic and Fikret Abdic from 15 May 1992. Miroslav Gagovic was a colonel in the JNA in Sarajevo and Fikret Abdic was a prominent political figure. At page 2 in B/C/S and English 3, from line 25, Gagovic said I'm not going -- this is Gagovic speaking on the phone to Fikret Abdic, and he said: "I'm not going into the matter of them having fire from the personal carriers which we took from Krtelj." Fikret Abdic asked: "Who has them?" Gagovic said: "Well, the Serbian Territorial Defence has them." And the next page in English. Gagovic says: "Police ones. They have six of them, like police ones. Those guys over there painted them. That's down there near the part towards Ilidza. It could be that those are, but my men were not. But they know each other. They have those recoilless guns installed up there. That's the difference compared to our personnel carrier. Our one did not." Mr. Ivanovic, as you can see, the Serbian Territorial Defence used the personnel carriers from Krtelj and they were shooting from them. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: JANKO IVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would offer this intercept into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well -- yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mr. President. Can the Prosecution confirm that this is one of those that has been part of their chart as having been authenticated?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Knowing the practice of the Chamber, what's the basis on your part to tender this intercept, Mr. Zec? In particular as regards the authenticity.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: As regards the authenticity, Your Honours, you remember that Mr. Gagovic testified on Tuesday, and he accepted as genuine all the intercepts that were presented to him. And those --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't remember that he was -- he commented upon this intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Not this particular one, but all other intercepts that he was speaker of and he confirmed the authenticity of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was he shown this intercept at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: This is the sort of the intercept that he was shown. And I refer your attention P06071, which is another intercept with Gagovic and Smajic of 11 May 1992. And if you compare these two intercepts, they -- the format is the same, the source that we got from is the same, and even commenting on Smajic -- Gagovic-Smajic intercept, Mr. Gagovic said that he remembered that intercept very well. That's on transcript page 31878. And there he also on transcript he referred that he was in contact and he talked to Abdic. And now we have another intercept four day later which is Mr. Gagovic and Abdic. Also, we can offer you audio recordings of these intercepts if you want to compare them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Would you like to add anything, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. In principle, we're not concerned about the reliability of these intercepts in a vacuum, but we want to make sure that the Defence intercepts and the Prosecution intercepts are treated the same, and so far it looks like the Defence intercepts are blocked by a feeling that unless they had been included in part of the Prosecution's evidence, despite the agreement that we had, that they will not be admitted and would not be considered reliable. So if that situation can be revisited, then we also don't see any reason why this couldn't otherwise be accepted as being reliable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll take this issue under advisement and give a ruling there due course. Please continue, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I have nothing further, Your Honour. Thank you very much. Thank you very much, Mr. Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ivanovic, earlier today you were asked, and that's on page 8, line 22, whether those soldiers slept at home, and then did they go to their positions outside of Hrasnica from their homes? In Hrasnica itself, were there any military facilities? Were there any firing positions, mortars, or front lines?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I believe --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were some, but I don't know where. In the direction of Vojkovici and in the direction of Ilidza. That's where the positions were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How far was that from Hrasnica?

utterances.speaker: JANKO IVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's on the border in the direction of Famos, the border between Hrasnica and Vojkovici, and in the direction of Ilidza it was close to the swimming pool near Ilidza from Tucevac [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you able to see or did you know about weapons or shots from Hrasnica, if there were any positions of the army in Hrasnica itself?

utterances.speaker: JANKO IVANOVIC
utterances.text: I -- I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You answered you didn't know that; right?

utterances.speaker: JANKO IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And can you please tell us if you know if there was any fighting in Hrasnica and around Hrasnica? Who was it who attacked, and what were the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: JANKO IVANOVIC
utterances.text: I know that the Muslim forces attacked Ilidza in April. I believe that it was on the 11th. They took the Serbs by surprise and 11 Serbian soldiers got killed on the occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it's very difficult to intervene in the circumstances where we are hearing witness's evidence via videolink, but I have difficulty to understand how your last questions arose from the cross-examination. Was that your point, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Exactly. This is beyond cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, with all due respect, Excellency --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please wrap up your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, Excellency, the Prosecutor implied that Hrasnica was a civilian settlement where soldiers only slept with their families, and then they left Hrasnica to go to their positions which were outside of Hrasnica. The position of the Defence is that Hrasnica was highly and densely militarised, and that is the basis for my questions based on the cross-examination. Please look at page 8, line 22.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you asked the question about the positions in Hrasnica, and the witness answered the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I just wanted to explain why I was asking that. Thank you, Mr. Ivanovic. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivanovic. That concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Chamber, I would like to thank you for your co-operation. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I think we are ready to go on with the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The next witness, also testifying by videolink, is Mr. Miscevic, and as soon as he can be in place we can continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was wondering whether the Chamber has at all been informed of the change of witness order.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Actually, the only change in the witness order was that there was one witness that we scheduled for yesterday in case we reached him, but the videolink was always fixed for this morning at 9.00, so we interrupted our order of witnesses to make sure that these two people testified at not -- beginning at 9.00 a.m., and then Mr. Vujcic who we thought might testify yesterday will testify immediately after these two videolink witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably that information hasn't reached me, but thank you. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We'll need just a couple of minutes to change positions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. But in the meantime, we could continue with the procedural matters, including the solemn declaration, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Certainly, I think so. If there's any delay following that, then we'll bring it to your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Mr. Miscevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it that you are hearing my words in your language well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you. I can. I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Miscevic. Please take your seat and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Miscevic.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you give my Defence team a statement?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Both you and I have to make pauses between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D5590 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this the statement that you provided to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you review that statement and does it accurately reflect your words?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you sign the statement?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you today in the courtroom, would your answers be the same as they are in the statement?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I am tendering this statement into evidence. I believe that there are associated documents pursuant to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we lost the connection at the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: After 40 minutes I think it's automatic, so it can be recalled.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, we're back on line, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Any question, Mr. Kosti [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: It's File. Mr. File.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ah, Mr. File. I'm sorry. Today I seem to be carried away. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. File?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I believe that we have the same situation as we did in the previous witness's case. I haven't seen any redactions done to this statement. The order of 21 November 2012, required the redaction of paragraphs, 5, 7, 13, and 14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me see. Will that redaction be carried out, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it will, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like a five minutes' break.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Actually, I sent an e-mail to my Case Manager to revise the summary about 15 minutes ago when I saw this problem come up with the other witness, so if he's been able to do that, I think we can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. So with that understanding, there's no objection from you?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: There is one additional issue related to the associated exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: This is 1D8553, which is a map. I've noticed that there are three items indicated on the map which either are not referred to in this statement or are part of the redacted portion of the statement. So I believe those three items should be redacted from the map as well. They --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we upload that map. For the benefit of the Chamber, can you identify the places that were included in para 7 and 14 that should be redacted?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Paragraph 7 refers to the item at the top which says garages where new prison for Serb civilians was established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: In the lower right-hand corner there is an indication of prison for Serb civilians. That comes from paragraph 14. And then in the far upper-left corner there's prison for Serb civilians, and unless I'm mistaken, that is not referred to anywhere in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: With the understanding that those three places you referred to are not relevant to this case, can we not admit this?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I would be happy for it to be admitted under those conditions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. With that caveat, we'll admit both the statement as well as the map. Shall we give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The statement shall be assigned Exhibit D2765, and the map shall be assigned Exhibit D2766. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm now going to read a summary of Mr. Miscevic's statement in English, and if I touch upon one of the paragraphs, 5, 7, 13, or 14, I beg your indulgence. [In English] Ilija Miscevic spent the war with his daughter in Hrasnica in the territory controlled by Muslim forces. Before the war, he would see armed Muslims in uniform, and at Kovaci he saw Muslims handing out weaponry publicly. They would search apartments. The central command of the 4th Motorised Brigade of the 1st Corps of BH Army was stationed in the central post office in Hrasnica. When the war started in April 1992, the Muslim forces began detaining Serbian civilians, including women, in the Aleksa Santic school, which became a prison for about a month before the Serb civilians were transferred to around 20 garages where a new prison was set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object to this again as referring to paragraph 7, the transfer of civilians to 20 garages. This was redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it this is not on purpose but out of mistake, but please be cautious in the future, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, I'll do my best, although my whole being is against it, because even Muslim settlements are presented as civilian settlements and Islam, and the Serbs are represented as the wolf. And that has an impact on the fairness of this trial and the perception the general public may get of this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's totally inappropriate. The Chamber has given its ruling as to the relevance of the part of the statement. This is not an opportunity to revisit the issue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Okay. I'll try to avoid all of that. The Muslim forces also had an annealing furnace in the gym and manufactured shells there. I skip something. Members of the 4th Motorised Brigade lived in Ilija Miscevic's skyscraper and carried their weapons with them. Ilija Miscevic saw a Muslim combatant firing shells in the direction of the Serbian territory from a truck with a mortar attached to it. An aerial bomb also hit -- also hit a house opposite to the school. I have to skip all other elements of this summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Miscevic, for the time being I don't have any questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Miscevic, as you have now noted, your evidence in chief in this case has been admit in writing, i.e., through your statement. Now you'll be cross-examined by the member of the Office of the Prosecutor. Mr. File.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Miscevic. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I'd like to turn your attention to Exhibit 65 ter 24391. Do you recognise this as a map of the area surrounding Hrasnica centre?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. But it is very small --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Please take a look -- if you would, please take a look at the four locations that are circled in red. You will see Bijela Kosa, Radeljevaca, Vrhovi, and Kotorni Cairi.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that. I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I would just like to ask you about the location --

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: I have never been here.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Do you recognise those areas as being located in the hills leading up to Mount Igman behind Hrasnica?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: I know nothing about this. I'm not familiar with these places at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I'm just asking you to look at the map and to see where they are located. Are you familiar with Mount Igman?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: Of course, I am. I have been there when I went to collect fuel wood. I know Igman but I've never been to any of these places here.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: But can you see these places on the map are between Hrasnica centre and Mount Igman?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see all those places.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Your Honours, for your own reference, these four locations represent the locations of the armaments of the ABiH 4th Motorised Brigade Mixed Artillery Battalion as described in D779 at the bottom of page 2 in the B/C/S and page 3 to 4 in the English, which is an SRK command order by Dragomir Milosevic dated 27 March 1995 describing four mortar platoons and one howitzer. I would tender that document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We object to that, and I think this last piece of information was really not something that was appropriate since it's not part of the evidence. It's a submission. So we don't think the witness has given any information that would justify the admission of the document, and the references to what the document depicts is not evidence from the Prosecutor and therefore shouldn't be considered by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: If I may respond briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. File.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: The description is not my own description. It's the description that appears of these places in Exhibit D779. The witness has confirmed that this is a map of the area surrounding Hrasnica, and therefore this is only tendered as an aid for the Tribunal to understand where those locations are.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: But the witness hasn't confirmed that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. File, the Chamber agrees with Mr. Robinson's observation. You may have different way in which you can tender the explanation based upon Exhibit D779. We'll not admit this one through this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Mr. Miscevic, I'd like to turn your attention to paragraph 10 of your statement. There you say I know an aerial bomb hit a house near Aleksa Santic school. Are we talking about the air-bomb attacking Hrasnica on 7 April, 1995?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what type of bomb that was, whether it was an aerial bomb or some other kind of bomb. I only heard an unknown sound, something like a ventilator close to my skyscraper, and a few seconds later I heard an explosion. I don't know anything else. I don't know what the bomb was. I don't know anything more about that. I only saw the place where it fell. I saw that it had a huge destructive power, and that's all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So just to be clear, when you said in your statement, "I know that an aerial bomb hit a house opposite the Aleksa Santic school," you in fact do not know that it was an aerial bomb. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. It fell. Some device fell, and its destructive power was much larger than the previously fired ten shells. There was a very loud detonation. I went by that house every day. I saw what the bomb had done to it. I don't know whether anybody was in the house when the bomb fell. I don't know whether anybody was killed. I learned later that that had been an aerial bomb or something of the kind. I only saw that house that was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Mr. Miscevic, in -- in your statement, you go on to say the owner of the house was a man named Lokvancic [phoen], and then you say the house was dilapidated and old and was in a very poor state.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us why did you feel it was necessary --

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. One of the most --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Mr. Miscevic. My question was: Why did you feel it was necessary to add this detail about the condition of the house? Are you trying to minimise the damage that was caused by the aerial bomb by claiming that the destroyed home was already in poor condition before it was blown up?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: No. No. Far from that. If it had fallen on my skyscraper, it may have destroyed half of it. It landed some 20 metres away of that. It hit that building by accident, and I don't even know whether there was anybody residing in it at the time. It was by accident. It was by accident that the bomb hit the oldest house. It may have hit the school or something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Mr. Miscevic, I'm afraid that wasn't my question. I was asking you why did you feel the need to add this detail about the condition of the house in your statement.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: I was not thinking about that at all. I just mentioned what I knew. That detail doesn't matter at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I'd like to discuss the map of Hrasnica that you mention in your statement, which was admitted as D2766. This map has a number of typewritten designations in English with red arrows pointing to particular buildings and locations. First of all, can you read and write in English?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So you -- so you did not personally create this map yourself?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: I only marked the locations where I reside, where the school is, where the bank used to be. All that is written in my statement. I showed the places and locations in Hrasnica because I know Hrasnica. I've been here for 60 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: My question was: You did not mark this exact map, did you? You marked a different map.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: I marked it here. Yes. Yes, this is the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So my question --

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: I marked it on this map. Right on this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So then my question would be you just testified that you could not read and write in English, but yet there are markings in English on this map. So you did not make those markings; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: No, not in English. I only marked the locations that I knew, and I marked it in the language that I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Can I turn your attention to 1D8562, which appears to be a handwritten map. Is this the map that you marked personally yourself?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: I drew this with my own hand, explaining positions in Hrasnica. I marked this in my own hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And was this the map that you gave to the Defence to form the basis for the map that we looked at previously?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw this map, because I found it difficult to orientate myself on the original map. That's why I made my own markings of the positions of the skyscraper where I live, the post office, and where the bank used to be, the features that I mentioned in my statement. And I did it quickly in my own hand, although if I had had more time, I could have done it better and in greater detail. This is just a part of all of this. I marked it in my own hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Mr. Miscevic, you just testified that on this handwritten map you marked the post office as well as the skyscraper where you used to live, but I'm afraid I'm having trouble seeing where you marked those locations. Could you indicate where on that map you marked those.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: Here is the skyscraper where I live. This is the skyscraper where the police was, and this is the post office where the command was located.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Is there -- is there anything written on this map which says "skyscraper" or "post office"?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: No. I did not write anything. I just marked locations. I didn't write anything. And on this other map that I drew, this is the building that I marked. That's the skyscraper where I live.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's return to that map D2766, because I'd like to ask you some questions about the post office?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. File. I noted that witness drew something or marked something on the map. Would you like to have it back or are you happy to continue without it?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I don't know if it's possible to see that from here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could the court deputy -- court deputy show the map marked to the camera.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes. The markings are right here. He circled. I'm not sure if it's visible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] The right --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please keep it just in case and then let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] And the witness has also marked -- also marked the sketch right here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Just keep them, both of them, just in case, and we'll continue how it goes. Please continue, Mr. File.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Now, looking at the map that was admitted, D2766, in the upper left hand quadrant of that map there is in capital letters "Post office, command for MTBR ABiH, and then further south and a little to the east there's a building circled and identified as Aleksa Santic school. And then if you go even further south into the east, you have a green dot and the number 10, which reflects the location of the air-bomb attack we were just discussing. Is this a correct reading of your map?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: You're asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: This is number 10, the school, and the air-bomb landed somewhere here, right here. I can't locate it precisely from these other features around, but it fell somewhere here near the school, not more than 100 metres from the school, to the east.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Is this the area marked as number 10 that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: Number 10 is the school. This is close by.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Looking at the map --

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: It's not marked here, but it's right here. It's not number 10. Number 10 is the school, Aleksa Santic school.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Now, I understand this to be a change to what is written on the map currently. If you look at where just below number 10 there's the word "Hrasnica," and below that is the word -- or the phrase "Aleksa Santic school" with a red arrow that points to --

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So are you saying this annotation, "Aleksa Santic school" with the red arrow, is not pointing to the correct location of the school?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's correctly marked. That is the house, number 10. Excuse me. That was the hotel or the community centre. There was also a cinema inside at number 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: You're saying that the area of number 10 represents a house and a cinema and a community centre?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: Number 10, that's the community centre or hotel, as you wish. The cinema, the library, and community rooms were inside at number 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And do you understand that to be the location where the bomb landed?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: It's a hundred metres to the east, further east towards Glamoc, 100 metres from the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. So if we assume that the air-bomb landed 100 metres to the east of this marking of number 10 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think witness said 100 metre from number 10. What he said, 100 metre from the school.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the school, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So where would that be in relation to the marking of number 10 on this map?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's be sure. Mr. File, could you be clearer by number 10? Do you mean the number 10 or the dot beside it?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Miscevic, I'm referring to the dot that is labelled number 10. Not the actual numbers but the dot.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: The source was here, the Hrasnica source, mineral source.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Mr. Miscevic, my question is simply whether that dot reflects the location where the bomb landed.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: It's here. That's where it landed. Somewhere here to the east. To the left of the school, that is, to the east, 100 metres, not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: You just said to the left of the school, that is to the east.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] If I might clarify, Your Honours. The witness is looking at the map upside down. I tried to turn it for him, but -- but he prefers to look at it upside down. So when he says it's to the left, it's to the left when you see it upside down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Doraiswamy. Please continue, Mr. File.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So if we assume that the location where the bomb landed is to the east of the dot that is indicated on this map --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure the witness said to the east of that dot. The witness said so. He said east of the school.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] East of the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know where that would be in relation to the green dot that's on the map?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Your Honours, I'm giving him the -- the witness the coloured map now. He was looking at the black and white version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that's the problem -- was the problem. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's here somewhere, in this area. That is it. It's somewhere in this area roughly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Miscevic, let me ask you, does -- do you hear me Mr. Miscevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you see the green dot Mr. Prosecutor referred to on the map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Does that place -- does that position reflect the location where the bomb landed at the time? He.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then where is the position where the bomb landed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] East. I marked it here. Somewhere in this area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Since we cannot see the marking --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it to the east of that green dot, Mr. Miscevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] East of the green dot. Perhaps 300 metres from the green dot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you see a school on the map, Mr. Miscevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see it. It says number 10 next to the school. There's a circle, and inside the circle is the school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, I'll leave it there. Mr. File, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So just to make sure that I understand what you're testifying about, the locations of three different items on this map, you have the post office a little bit to the north and west of the area we were just looking at, you have the school which you've marked, which is to the south of the post office, and then you have the location where the bomb landed, which you said is to the east of the green dot.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. From my skyscraper to the south is the school. It's not marked correctly here. This is the Aleksa Santic school. And number 10 is the community centre. Between the school and the community centre, 100 metres to the east is where the bomb fell. That house is not drawn here.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to read you a sentence of testimony from a Defence witness Ilidza Brigade commander Vladimir Radojcic from 12 December, 2012. This was at transcript page 31267. In his testimony he said: "In the information I got from UNPROFOR and the people who had fled Sarajevo, the air-bomb that was launched landed exactly between the school and the post office building." Now, looking at the map that you made --

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I would also like --

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I would also like to refer you to Exhibit D2562. This is the witness statement from that same witness. And I'm going to ask for page 5 of the B/C/S and page 4 of the English. Now, I'm just showing you so you can read along in paragraph 20, in the middle of paragraph 20 he says: "On document 1D8396, I marked with a square the post office in Hrasnica in which the command of the 104 MTBR Motorised Brigade of the BHA 1 K was accommodated. The post office was located in the very centre of Hrasnica. On the same document, 1D8396, I marked with a circle the building of the Aleksa Santic school." Now I'm going to show you that map which is Exhibit D2590. So here you see the building in the middle with the square around it that -- that Witness Radojcic said was the post office, and you see the building with the circle that he said was the school. Now, according to you, this map is also incorrect because the square that indicates the post office is indicating the wrong building; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Have we passed another 40 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Mr. Miscevic, my question to you is does that building with the square around it --

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: This square -- this square here is the community centre. The school is this ellipsis or circle.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just have two final brief areas of questions that thankfully do not require the use of the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Mr. Miscevic, in paragraph 8 of your statement you said the Muslims manufactured shells in the gym of the Aleksa Santic school, and then you add that there was an annealing furnace in the gym which was used for annealing shells. Did you see this with your own eyes or did you hear this from someone?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: I saw that. I know that. That was only the steeling, whereas the production was in garages between those two skyscrapers, mine and where the commander was. Those were -- that was an underground car park. There were several machines in there, and workers came every day, and I saw some of my friends who worked there every day. That was no secret. Everybody who lived in the neighbourhood saw that, and they returned those processed shells by forklifts back to their -- the other installation for steeling.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to read to you again the testimony of Colonel Radojcic, this time from the 11th of December, 2012, at transcript page 31258, lines 11 and 12. He says the -- he describes the school as "the place where ammunition was being manufactured for a little while during the war." Do you agree with this characterization that it was manufactured for a little while?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: No. There was no production going on in the school. The only thing that was going on was melting in the gym, a manufacturing process took place somewhere else. And I've already told you that. That was next to my skyscraper in the basement, next to the place where I resided. That workshop was 10 metres away from my apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I'd like to move to paragraph 9 of your statement where you say that you saw with your own eyes a Muslim combatant nicknamed Kamlica [phoen] firing shells in the direction of the Serbian territory from a truck that had a mortar attached to it that was near your skyscraper. In that part of your statement you say that he would flee and then take shelter elsewhere and that the Serbian side would return fire five to ten minutes later. And you say that this happened several times and that your skyscraper was quite damaged. Where were you when you were observing this?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: From my balcony I saw all that. I lived on the fifth floor. But I didn't see it several times. I saw that truck, and I saw that fire was opened from it, but I know that it was in the -- in the Serb direction. Very soon there was a response and shells started falling around the skyscraper, but who responded to that fire I don't have a clue. I realized only later that there was some technology involved that could locate it, the place from which it was fire, but very quickly it would move and it would be hid in a garage or a sheltered place. And I saw that with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Mr. Miscevic, just to be clear, you say in your statement that this happened several times, and you also say in your statement that the Serbian side would return fire five to ten minutes later; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: The Serb side opened fire every day. One has to be fair and say that. But when fire was opened from Hrasnica - I don't know in what direction - very soon there would be a response, maybe ten minutes later. A response would arrive every time. So there were casualties, civilian casualties, in my skyscraper, casualties of all ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: What kind of weapons do you know were used to respond? Were there artillery gun shells?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: Mostly shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Were there --

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: Mostly shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Were there also mortar shells?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: All sorts of shells fell on my skyscraper, but mostly mortar shells in response.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: How many times was your own skyscraper hit?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: My apartment was hit six or seven times, for example, but the skyscraper itself was hit over a hundred times.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And you were living in your apartment with your daughter as well?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I still live there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that each time your building was hit by shells that you and your daughter were terrified?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: My daughter was in the basement. I, however, could not be in the basement, because I had been operated upon previously. I had received radiotherapy, and that's why I was in my apartment. Of course I was scared. I was in my apartment three or four times when heavy artillery, perhaps even a tank -- tanks opened fire on my apartment. However, I was only slightly wounded. I can even say that I was not injured, but my apartment was seriously damaged as a result.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I have no more questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, four or five questions, Excellency. It can be done quickly, but if you want us to have a break first, we can do that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you think you can finish your re-examination in five minutes?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please go on, Mr. Karadzic, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Miscevic, I will try to do it as fast as possible. What was in the Aleksa Santic school during the war? Did school -- kids go to school?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: No. Kids didn't go to school, because it was just a military department. Under the staircase there was a group of detained civilians. They called that area a prison. There was nothing else there. There were no troops there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what about the Dom? What was that during the war?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: It was just a mess. It was where food was prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the municipality. On the upper floors, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. File.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I don't believe the Dom was discussed in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was wondering whether witness said at a certain point of time Dom at all. I think I heard in B/C/S. What does Dom -- could we clarify with the assistance of the interpreters whether -- Mr. Miscevic, did you ever say about the Dom in your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. When I pointed to the Dom or the community centre on the map. During the war, that's where food was prepared. Serbian workers would go there and eat there together with the troops -- I also went there to eat if I was working that day. I would go to the community centre, to the Dom, to eat there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And this is a question for the interpreter from myself. Could "Dom" in B/C/S be translated as "community centre" in English?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It is a community centre, Your Honours, the interpreter notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you happy with this clarification, Mr. File?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you say food was prepared, who was it prepared for?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: For the troops and for the work platoon, for the people who were digging trenches and doing other things. There were two groups of Serbs who were digging trenches, and then they would come to Hrasnica, and they would eat there. They would receive one meal a day there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I suppose it should be -- said "served" and not "prepared," "food was served over there."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's where food was served and the troops would go and eat there, right?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that your daughter would go down to the basement during shelling. At what point in time would she go to the basement? How did you know that shelling would take place?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: There was an alert and everybody had to go to the basement. That's where we stayed. That's where we slept. We would spend the entire day there. And not only my daughter but everybody from the skyscraper. I was the only one, perhaps the only one who was in the apartment during shelling. I would rarely go down to the basement because I was sick.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. Let's drop that. Some things remained unclear with regard to the map. Did you enter anything on the map? Did you also tell us what those things were? Or was it somebody else who made the markings?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: I pointed at the places and all of them where they were, and they made the markings. I didn't do it with my own hand. I only pointed to the place where I lived, I pointed to the community place, the school, the post office, the bank. I pointed to some interesting places, places of interest for the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you happy with the way things were recorded?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: There were some ambiguities on the map that I was shown. In reality, there are some differences. It was an older map. That map preceded the markings by some 10 or 15 years. Between the buildings on the map there are a lot more buildings that were constructed before the war. For example, the post office where -- where I received my monies, also some shops, and there were a lot of buildings that were not depicted on the map, which is why I found it difficult to find my bearings on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But do you still believe that what was marked was correctly marked?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA MISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was marked correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Miscevic, for your testimony. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Miscevic. That concludes your evidence. On behalf of the --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Your Honours, sorry, would you like the witness to sign and date the three documents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think it's necessary. Mr. File, can I hear from you?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I don't think it's necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Court Deputy. That concludes your evidence, Mr. Miscevic. On behalf of the Chamber, I'd like to thank you for your co-operation. Now you're free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll take a break for half an hour and resume at 20 past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, before he does that, may I introduce Danko Kostovic, who is one of our case managers who is joining us this session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Vujicic, do you hear me in your language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you kindly make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vujicic. Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Vujicic.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: First of all, let me ask you to pause before you start giving your answer. I have to remind myself of the same for the benefit of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: I shall certainly do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you provided a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could like to call up 1D07011 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this the statement, the one you see on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you about some ambiguities with regard to the years. In paragraph 3, it says that in September of 1991, the Serbian Democratic Party was set up in Foca. Was that in 1991, after the elections, or was it actually set up in 1990, before the elections?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: I know very well that the Serbian Democratic Party was established in Foca. It was publicly announced in September of 1991 at the stadium in Foca. Much later than the Party of Democratic Action was set up if Foca, in Donje Polje, on the right bank of the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now can we look at paragraph 11. I would like you to clarify something for us in paragraph 11. That will be on page 3.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll be waiting for your questions. It's very difficult for me to find the paragraphs myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please look at paragraph 11 where you say that in the so-called Partizan sports facility there were a lot of civilians, exclusively women. And before that, you say that Muslims were protected by your guards. Who were those female civilians which were protected at the Partizan Sports Hall?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: That sports hall is some hundred metres away from the building where I resided at the time and where I still reside. I was not mobilised. I didn't carry a gun, because I was too old, but I was requested to assist with something. I know that a commissioner appointed me to stand guard on some nights next to the Partizan Sports Hall. It's a miniature sports hall. I was given a rifle on those occasions, and I was told that mostly women were kept there. I don't know how old. I don't know how many. They were inside. I never opened the door. It was during the night hours, and we were told that those civilians had to be guarded while we were on duty. I had a rifle, and I was told that if somebody tried to force their way into the facility, you had to warn him first and then you can open fire. However, luckily enough while I stood guard for those three or four nights, nobody came. Nobody tried to enter. I did not have to clash with anybody. Those women, if they were indeed women - they probably were - they never tried to leave that facility. I can tell you why the female population was there. When the conflicts ended in Foca and when calm returned to Foca, the focus of armed conflict shifted to the villages in Foca municipality. Foca municipality was one of the biggest in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. A wide theatre of war was opened, and not every house, not every piece of the territory could be covered. And in any war, undesired consequences may be expected, so the village population, the infirm and fable [as interpreted], and the civilians were recommended for their own safety to go to the Partizan Sports Hall, and that's where the females decided to go in order not to be disturbed. So those village women arrived there? And as far as I know, during the day those females could leave those facilities, whereas during the night hours there were guards who guarded them. Sometime in the second half of April, I was mobilised as some other people remained. They stood guard, and they received the same instructions as I did. I don't know what transpired next.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did I understand you properly? Were those Muslims from the villages that were affected by conflicts?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. Those people came from villages that were some 10 to 15 kilometres away from Foca. Neither Serbian forces nor the police could guarantee their safety. They could not promise them that they wouldn't go unscathed. When the Muslim armed forces left those villages, they remained unprotected, and those of the people who were left behind were women and elderly. Men would be accommodated in some other facilities where they were protected. For example, they were accommodated in the penal institute. There were Serbs and Muslims there, and they were some of the convicts who had been tried before the war, whereas the female population was accommodated in some facilities where there was room as a rule. When it comes to Foca and the female population that remained there, the civilian authorities, i.e., the police, secured those houses which housed a large number of women. For example, in Mahala, there were two or three women in a house. Then one night a guard was appointed. He carried a rifle. A paramilitary arrived from somewhere and tried to break in -- into that house. That was in the month of April. The guard warned him several times. The -- that person did not want to listen. The guard opened fire and killed that paramilitary. What I'm trying to say is that that person was given the same instruction as those who stood guard in front of the Partizan Sports Hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: After all those clarifications, would you say your statement is the accurate reflection of your words?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes. I just related those things that I saw with my own eyes and things that are true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you sign the statement?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I stand by it. I did not give the statement under duress.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to put the same questions to you today, the same ones that were put to you before you gave your statement, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: I suppose that they would be. Maybe in the meantime, there -- I have remembered some other things. If you asked me some different questions or if you put your questions differently, maybe I would remember some other details.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this package, and I will have a few questions after I read the witness's statement summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Good morning everyone. Yes. Indeed. I have already sent an e-mail to all sides and have requested that paragraph 4 of this statement be excluded. Yesterday, in two oral decisions related to the witness Pljevaljcic, you ordered the exclusion of paragraphs from the statement dealing with the Focatrans affair in 1998 and 1990, and here paragraph 4 deals with this very same event in very similar terms, although shorter, and I would like this paragraph to be excluded, because there is no relevance to this trial.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We agree in the light of your decision regarding this issue. The Defence accepts this objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think all of that paragraph deals with Focatrans events, so I would order the first two sentences to be redacted from the paragraph. But in addition to this one, I note, Mr. Karadzic or Mr. Robinson, six paragraphs have been added after the proofing with this witness, but I found some of the translations incomprehensible. Examples of those sentences are second sentence of para 28, fourth sentence of para 29, and the third sentence of para 33. So I would order the -- a revised translation to be uploaded as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll do that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So with that understanding, we'll admit the Rule 92 ter statement of this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit D2767. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to read a summary of Mr. Vujicic's statement in English. [In English] Milutin Vujicic was a guard at the Partizan hall in Foca and a soldier until May 1994. In mid-1991, he attended meetings of the SDA in its formation and noted the provocative nature of the meeting particularly in relation to the topics of Serbian Foca and Serb people. The leader Alija Izetbegovic said that BH had to be an independent state, and if people did not want this, they should go and live in another area. The SDS was not set up until September 1991. At a rally a number of representatives from the other parties and municipalities were invited to attend and given the chance to speak, an opportunity that was not afforded to the SDS at the others' rallies.
