The rally was not provocative in nature, and for the first year the parties co-existed. Before the fighting broke out, an incident occurred at Foca -- mm-hmm. That is out. I'll skip it. At that time, Muslim officers and soldiers who were in military service discontinued and discharged their military service and instead joined the Green Berets. The Green Berets were under the command of the BH Army, and members of this organisation appeared on the street -- streets before the fighting started. People also began arming themselves at that point -- at this point, and the Muslims armed themselves much earlier than the Serbs and many underwent military training in 1991. Serbian people began arming themselves very late in 1992, usually only with rifles or light infantry weapons seized from the depots of the former JNA. Milutin Vujicic saw Muslim forces fighting from several mosques, and he also saw a call for Muslim personnel to place themselves at the disposal of the Green Berets. There were rumours of splitting Foca along ethnic lines and the clashes began when the -- when the misunderstandings culminated. The Muslim forces torched several Serbian houses in April 1992. Foca was liberated by Serb forces from Muslim paramilitaries a few days later. There were no paramilitary formations from the Republic of Serbia near Foca. However, there were other paramilitary formations nearby, and these caused Serbian people a lot of harm. Milutin Vujicic saw that measures were taken to protect the Muslim population of Foca municipality from paramilitaries. Inhabitant of distant villages where Muslim forces could not be -- when the paramilitaries could not be controlled, were brought to the town and placed in certain facilities where they could be defended. Many of these people were women and children. Some were housed in the Partizan sports facility which he guarded himself. If residents wished to remain in their properties, they were able to do so but were warned of the danger from the paramilitaries. Vrbnica village, Serbian village, was completely razed to the ground on 8th of April, 1992. Many more soldiers were called up in May 1992 as the Foca municipality was not able to defend all of the borders and Muslim forces were entering Serbian villages and committing heinous crimes. Before being sent to the front line, Milutin Vujicic read the rules of conduct of the Serbian armed forces which contained provisions of the Geneva Conventions on war and conflicts. These provisions were announced again to all the soldiers before they left ensuring that they were away of them. Further, the soldiers were told that when mopping up villages from Muslim paramilitaries, the civilian population and their farms, houses, and other mobile and immobile property were completely off limits and every transgression strictly punished. Many Muslim inhabitants began leaving Foca. They asked to leave, requested -- and requested that their relocation be protected by -- both of these were granted. The Muslims were not forced to leave and were made aware of this fact. However, they did this voluntarily. During the year in which Milutin Vujicic fought on the front line, the soldiers were attacked several times by the Muslim armed formations from in front of and also from behind. However, the army carried out mainly defensive operations. After the withdrawal of the JNA, the Republika Srpska armed forces mainly took infantry weapons from the JNA depots in the territory. Muslim forces took heavier weapons from the depots which were used against the Serb population. No trenches were dug in Foca. These were only dug on the front line. There was no heavy artillery around Foca. The armed forces around Foca had no artillery, and the only the tank that the Serb forces had was one that had been left by the JNA as it was damaged. This had to be repaired by the Serbian forces and acquitted -- acquired in June 1992. [Interpretation] That would be the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you, Mr. Vujicic, do you know you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I forgot to ask you, Mr. Vujicic, to tell me at any point of time if you do not hear the proceedings well or you feel uncomfortable at any point in time. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear well only when questions are being asked. The rest of the sound has some interference in it. I can only answer questions from any party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. And please speak slow for the benefit of the interpreters and us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Sometimes I get carried away. But I understand very well. I know what interpreting is. I know it's a very hard job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just a few more questions, Mr. Vujicic. Is the name Senad Sahimpasic, nickname Saja, familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's very familiar. That's a man who was born in Foca. Began his studies. As far as I know he did not complete them. He started with trade in agricultural produce, fruit and vegetables, and he was doing very fell in Foca. He became a wealthy man. But I know that very early on, even before the 1990s, in 1989 he became politically active in the Muslim community and he was the first president of the SDA party in Foca. I know him still. He lives in Ustikolina nowadays. Ustikolina is a local commune of the former municipality of Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you Mr. Sahimpasic have a warehouse -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction:

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did he have a publication, a publishing house?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did publish a newspaper. It was a Muslim nationalist newspaper that published stories which disrupted the co-existence and unity between Serbs and Muslims in Foca. He published political platforms, announced to Muslims how very soon a new sovereign Muslim dominated Bosnia would be formed, and if the Serbs do not accept that, things are in store for them, all sorts of things, and this newspaper was called "Fokus," "Fokus." Before 1991, I road a story in "Fokus," a programme of 12 points listing what would happen to Serbs if they don't accept such developments in Bosnia. I can even tell you about some of these 12 points and what exactly they said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show 1D07558, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What do you see on the screen, Mr. Vujicic?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: This is this newspaper "Vox." "Vox." I remember this story, and I remember this picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And whose heads are those at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: They look like Chetniks with these fur hats. They look like Chetnik hats. And the man with his foot on somebody's head is dressed in Turkish costume with a typical hat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we see page 41.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's just a story I remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Vujicic. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we were not notified that any other exhibit except for the statement would be used with this witness. I do not really see why now we are presented with this kind of pamphlet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. What is your response to this, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My mistake. I apologise, and I kindly ask for flexibility, because we always try to be flexible in similar situations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And we have no translation, and it's difficult to follow.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a translation. We can put it on the ELMO. I only want the witness to confirm that that is indeed the story and how it affected the spirits in Foca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I will consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. The Chamber will allow you to continue this time. Shall we put the English translation on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Until then, please read this and then us, Mr. Vujicic, if this is indeed the story and how it affected spirits and the general atmosphere in Foca.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: I can read it, although I remember it so well. This was published in "Vox," this newspaper published and financed Sahimpasic known as Saja. It says: "What is in store for Serbs in Islamic Bosnia-Herzegovina?" It reads: "The day is coming closer when the announced proclamation of the Islamic Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina will happen. This date for which every Bosnian-Herzegovinian and Sandzak Muslim heart beats is, as we already know, the 31st of December this year. According to some indications, Bosnia-Herzegovina Serbs might oppose this historic happening."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujicic, I believe for all the other participants there is a translation available on another screen, so you don't need to read it. Just tell us how this affected the people in Foca.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: This is not the only story of its kind, but this one had a horrible impact on the peaceful relations between Muslims and Serbs living in the municipality of Foca. I know very well that some sober, reasonable Muslim intellectuals condemned this sort of writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I tender this page and the cover page of "Vox" magazine, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have not established yet, at least I didn't see it, when this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we see the first page. It says October 1991. Is it correct? Is it published in October 1991, Mr. Vujicic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This could have been 1990. As far as I remember, it was 1990, towards the end of 1990, October or September. It was published in one issue of this "New Vox" magazine.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see page 41 again, and zoom in on the preamble, see what's written there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Since this part has not been translated, could you read it for us, or shall I?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Read it yourself. I don't see very well, and these glasses are not really good.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It reads: "A year ago, our magazine published a funny story, a humourous story, about the relation of the so-called Islamic Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Ever since that time, our publication has been targeted by all sorts of manipulation, erroneous and malicious interpretations, peaking in the writing that we are publishing in this issue."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter cannot really follow, because it's not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The interpreters are not following you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Following our hoax, we have seen a development of the fascistoid position of Serbs in that so-called Islamic republic. Who is behind this, we do not know. Is it the Serbs trying to mobilise their population again, or could it be a Muslim provocation against Serbs, or is it perhaps a Croat attempt to cause a quarrel between Muslims and Serbs? It remains to be seen."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujicic, has this been seen as a hoax among the Serbs, and was it indeed a hoax?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: This was not a hoax. This was a serious piece of writing, and this whole story and all that I have been shown, all that I have seen, impacted on one incident that had a lot of influence on relations between Serb and Muslim workers in the Focatrans enterprise, a very large enterprise. And that incident led to increasing tensions between Muslims and Serbs in that area. Let me not speak about the Focatrans incident. That's a separate story.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that in 1991 this text was reprinted, and it was first published earlier?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: I read it in 1990, but when it was first published, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We can go back to page 1 again. Could you read the writing in red in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: "Handzar Division is ready."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is the Handzar Division?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: We can find references to the Handzar Division in writings about the Second World War, and in this conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina there have been all sorts of manipulations referring to the Handzar Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who was the Handzar Division made up of and on what side did it fight on?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: On the side of the occupier, and it was mainly made up of Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not relevant. Do you object to the admission of this page, 41, as well as page 1, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I suggest that it be marked for identification, and I would reserve my right to object later on when I can see it in full, because at the moment I'm a bit confused what is really -- is it a satirical thing or whatsoever. So I suggest to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. And what does "Vox" mean in B/C/S, Mr. Vujicic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've never given it any thought. It says "New Vox." It has a crescent in the letter O, a Turkish symbol.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's how I would interpret it. I cannot interpret it in any other way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will mark it for identification as Exhibit D2768, the first page and page 41 of this magazine. I understand that Defence will upload only those two pages, excluding all the remaining pages.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Vujicic. Those were all my questions for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Vujicic, your evidence has been admitted in most part in the writing, and you'll be further asked by the Prosecutor in its cross-examination. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Vujicic.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In your statement, in paragraph 2, you refer to the SDA rally in Foca having taken place in mid-1991, and in the next paragraph, 3, you refer to the SDA founding rally September 1991. And Mr. Karadzic has already asked you about whether you were mistaken about the year, and if I understand your answer correctly, you say it was both in 1991. Is my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Vujicic, I'm afraid we are not hearing any interpretation. Could you kindly repeat your answer, Mr. Vujicic, from the beginning. Your answer was not translated, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will. The first political party in Foca was established and promoted in the local commune Donje Polje between two bridges on the right bank of the Drina, in an area called Pijesak. It was the promotion of the SDA party. It took place in the end of June or perhaps early July.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And which year?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we -- I would like to have a video played, and it is 65 ter 40496. And it's only very, very brief.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was that said to me?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, it was not said to you. It was actually said to Mr. Reid next to me to play a video. And before it is being played, it is, in fact, a video -- it's a video from the SDA founding rally that you just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: B, yes, B.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: A bit further.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: There should actually be some sound. And the sound ... We would have to hear the reporter speaking about what we are seeing here, and unfortunately there's no sound, but according to the -- the transcript that I have, the reporter is saying: "Inaugural meeting of the SDA in Foca was held on 25th August 1990." It's unfortunate it's not heard, but perhaps if the Defence would agree that the date would in fact have been the 25th of August, 1990, then we could solve that situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How about putting that question to the witness on the basis that the audio says this is an inaugural meeting of the SDA in Foca, which was held on 25th of August, 1990? Do you agree with it, Mr. Vujicic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would not agree to 1990. It was in 1991, although it's possible that -- I don't know. It was a long time August. In July or August, perhaps, but all I know is it was in 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be of assistance? I believe the witness is confusing a political rally that was a post-electoral rally in 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we leave it there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Vujicic, you also in paragraph 3 of your statement, you mention that while the members of the SDA were invited to the SDS rally and address the audience, the SDS representatives did not attend the SDA rally. In fact, were not even invited. Do you remember that you said that? In your statement, in paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: I said that in my previous statement. I said I don't remember that, and I don't think there was a single Serbian politician or leader invited to the SDA rally in Han Pijesak. It was a very loud rally on the right bank of the Drina involving 150 buses full of people. The police congregated on Foca --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sir, let me interrupt you. We just need a few -- few things, not your whole story. And you attended the SDA rally, is that --

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Sorry. I hear this speech in a foreign language at the same time as you are speaking, and I cannot follow the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. I would like -- I would ask our usher to take a look into the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That may have something to do with the volume of the headphone, but let's try again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's much better now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you hear me well now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can. I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. Vujicic, did you attend the SDA rally yourself?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: I did not go to Pijesak. I was on the other bank of the Drina where the buses were. That's perhaps a hundred metres away. There was also a public address system so I could hear everything, the presentation of their platform and programme, all the speeches, everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And as you heard all the speeches, did you not hear Mr. Velibor Ostojic attend and give a speech?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: No, I did not hear him speak at all. I don't know whether he spoke, but I didn't hear it. I don't even know whether he was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we try now the same -- the same video but now a different excerpt, and I hope that this time it works. It is 65 ter 40496A.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Several cities of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The guests of the Assembly in Foca were representatives of --"

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can you -- can we please start again so that we can hear what the anchor person says.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Several cities in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Guests of the Foca Assembly were representatives of the Serbian Democratic Party, Mr. Velibor Ostojic, president of the SDS Executive Board for Bosnia-Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we just move back where we hear that person speaking, the previous speaker speaking here.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Several cities in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Guests --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me stop here. Mr. Vujicic, that's Mr. Ostojic; right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: You mean the one at the roster? It is possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So, sir, Mr. Ostojic did attend the rally and did speak about it; correct -- sit on it, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: I never saw Ostojic in person. I only saw him on television. I never had an occasion to meet him in person.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to have this small clip admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Could you identify later on the time-frame of this video later on?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: To the registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit P6078. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please be told where the rally took place? Where was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Am I supposed to answer?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The witness has actually correctly identified it to be at the arena --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Han Pijesak?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's in Foca and it's at the conference of the rivers Drina and Cehotina, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Vujicic, the Trial Chamber has made a decision that we are not talking about the Focatrans affair. However, in paragraph 4 of your statement, you refer to an event that as you put broke out -- just before the war in Foca broke out Serbian employees had a strike and that then the Special Police from republic -- from the republic level Herzegovina intervened and beat up citizens.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's my understanding that this evidence is still tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. In -- in this context, I would like to have Exhibit 65 ter 24375 brought up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And as it is coming up, it is a press release by the Foca police station regarding a police intervention on the 11th of September, 1990. The date is actually -- can be seen on the next page. Can we please have the next page in both languages. And can we -- yes. Thank you. Are you again mistaken about the date, Mr. Vujicic? The event was the intervention of the police against strikers. Was that not in September 1990 and not just before the outbreak of the war?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Well, I personally think that the events at Focatrans started in 1989 and went on for some two years. I can see that this report dates back to 1990. I don't remember the details of the date. I only remember that in the morning when I went to work I came across police forces that started to persecute the population. I don't know whom precisely, but I suppose that they were after the workers who had walked out after they were fired by the management of Foca transport. They continued to work for a year. They set up their own company called Viner, and they operated it for a year. However, the Serbs set up a commission --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Vujicic, we don't want to speak about the details. We just want to speak about the police operation that you mentioned in your statement and to establish why it took place and when.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have again page 1 of -- in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: As you can see here, there is a reference in paragraph 2 that there was a ban of public rallies in Foca according to an order from the republic SUP. And if we go down a bit to the second last paragraph, it says here, and I read it to you as you said your glasses are not so good: "Despite pejorative and insulting words that were said to the police members, we tried to push the masses. However, when they became aggressive and commenced with physical attacks and throwing stones at the police, we used the water cannon, and when not even this yielded the result, we used rubber batons and tear gas, all with the aim to reject the attack and disperse the rally." Mr. Vujicic, is that now how it really happened and how it started? There was violence from both sides, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: I'll try and explain and make things clearer for you or, rather, to make them absolutely clear. I'll try to be brief and up to the point. First of all, the Executive Board of Bosnia and Herzegovina set up a commission that came to Foca and suspended all the civilian authorities and took matters in their hands. All those who had walked out, all those who had appropriated funds and equipment and continued to use them for a year in the newly established company Viner --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: -- they had all these things seized from them by the commission and --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sir, let me interrupt you. The only question we are talking about is the -- is the police intervention you mentioned that took place immediately before the war, and I put to you and which is from this police report, that it was in September 1990, and it was something that started with a ban of the rally and the police doing their job and then violence occurred.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Very well. What I'm trying to say is that it was not the Foca police. It was Special Police commanded by Commander Vikic, Special Police which was set up at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They were the ones who took the matters in their hands and implemented all those measures. I was an eyewitness of all that. I was the president of the biggest local commune in Foca, Gornje Polje at the time. I attended the meetings of that commission, and that's how things transpired. At the end they invited the Special Police from Sarajevo who did all those things. I could not even pass through the streets to go to work because of all those police officers. There were workers there with Beetles, some of them brought their own lorries, and all those were seized from them. They chased them for kilometres down the street. I don't know if people were stoned, but as far as I could see, as far as I knew, there was not that many stones thrown to provoke such reaction. Some were beaten up, and some succumbed to the wound as a result of the beating. Some -- some died. If you're not satisfied with my answer, please go on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sir, will you please go a bit further down. It says here if you look at the last paragraph: "Data indicating that only three persons requested medical aid during the day yesterday and two of whom directly who participated." There is no word from people who died. This is just not right. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: It is correct that on that day nobody was killed. However, people were beaten. Some women were beaten even --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: -- who had never been on any strike. They were just there on the street, and if they uttered a single word, they were beaten with batons. I saw that with my own --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: -- own two eyes. I can even tell you who the woman was that was beaten black and blue.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sir, let me interrupt you. At that time in 1990, the Foca police was not divided yet. It was all ethnic groups; right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes, but that Foca police -- the secretariat of the interior was a municipal secretariat. However, when that commission arrived and when those men took over, it was no longer the municipal police. They took the matters in their own hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, I'm sorry to interrupt you, but speaking for myself, I'm not quite sure still whether this document is referring to the same event referred to in her -- in his statement. The third sentence, i.e., the event in which Serbian --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I could read, I can see there are a lot of lies in here. Somebody wrote this report the way it suited him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Vujicic, I was asking a question to Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. Third sentence says: "Just before the war in Foca broke out, Serbian employees broke off and formed their own enterprises for transport of goods and passengers." Is this document referring to the same event? That was my question.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's the same event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether the witness confirmed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No. The witness seems to be definitely mistaken about the year. That is something that we actually heard already starting when Mr. Karadzic asked question. It's the event in 1990 that both this witness and the next one were talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If it is related to 1990 event, then that paragraph could go in its entirety as greed upon by Mr. Milosevic at first. But I -- when we read the same paragraph, it seems to be related to other than 1990.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had actually understood it always to be the same event, and when you compare with the next witness who is coming, it's indeed the same event, and I just tried to establish that with the witness. And I understood that Mr. Karadzic understood it also to be the event in 1990.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue then, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be heard on something? May I say something about this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vujicic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly, yes. First of all, they were all dismissed. The workers, the drivers, primarily those who had permanent contracts. They were all dismissed. Later on they set up their own company because they had been fired and they no longer benefitted from any workers' rights due to them by Focatrans.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Did that all take place at the same time, I mean in the same year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After 20 years, I really can't say whether it was in 1991 or in 1990, that is possible. I can't be sure really. I only know that those things happened. I saw them happening. I was an eyewitness. It was in the early morning hours. As I was on my way to work, I observed the entire situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, I take it you need more time to conclude your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. To clarify these particular points. It took a lot of time, and basically the main points -- some main points are still coming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, I was just wondering whether to take a break now or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And I cannot manage to do this in -- the entire cross-examination in half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It will take a bit longer, so sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we will take a break now for 45 minutes and resume at 20 past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, I would like to tender this exhibit into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit P6079. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Vujicic, in paragraph 6 of your statement, you refer to the fighting, and you state that the Serb forces liberated Foca from Muslim paramilitaries in less than five days. That's correct; right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And today and also in paragraph 26, 27, and 29 of your statement, you also gave more details on the fighting and you stated that Foca was not attacked with artillery. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Well, not really. However, when the conflict broke out, there was a device in Sukovac near Radio Foca tower. It was a kind of Verber [phoen] or a Russian Kacusa which fired at the Serbian population. They inflicted more or less damage. We found one that had fallen in Cehotina, and one had actually fallen on my brother's house. It was a man made device. On the Serbian side there was infantry weapons, an occasional Zolja, an occasional Osa. I don't know whether there was a recoilless gun or not. Later, at first there was nothing. At first Serbs only had rifles in their hands. For those few days or so I was in the basement of my house.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Vujicic, there's evidence before this Court that the Serbs' forces in Foca included the JNA units and that JNA units participated in the fight in Foca with artillery. And let me cite adjudicated fact 741 from the Krnojelac trial judgement, paragraph 20, to you, and it says: "Sometime between 8.30 and 10.00 on 8 April 1992, the main Serb attack on the Foca town began with a combination of infantry fire and shelling from artillery weapons in nearby Kalinovik and Miljevina, and Serb forces included local soldiers as well as soldiers from Montenegro and Yugoslavia, and in particular, a paramilitary formation known as the White Eagles. Mr. Vujicic, is that not how it happened on the 8th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: On the 8th of April, 1992, an armed conflict started. It involved Muslims and Serbs on the right bank of the Drina River above Foca in the immediate vicinity of villages inhabited by the Serbian population exclusively. I can tell you that that's where the first skirmishes and conflicts broke out, and that the Serb forces enjoyed some advantages in those conflicts. And the conflict spilled out from the slopes of the mountain to the city itself, and from one house to the next, from one apartment block to another apartment block. The conflict spread. And I know that the Muslim forces defended themselves from those residential buildings, from the mosques, from the wells. I know that there was a lot of weapons in the mosques.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sir, let me interrupt you here. I was actually asking you about the artillery, the JNA artillery, that shelled Foca from Kalinovik and Miljevina. That was actually the point I asked you, because you had denied that in your statement.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Hello? I was an eyewitness. I don't know whose artillery it was. In any case, shells fell from the direction of Miljevina, but not on Foca but on Sukovac and the forests on the right bank of the Drina. Not a single shell fell on Foca. I was there in my apartment -- or, rather, in my residential building. Not a single shell fell on Foca. Not a single shell hit a single facility in Foca, either a Muslim or a Serbian facility.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the White Eagles, they were from Serbia and they participated; right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: You're talking about trenches? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No. I was asking you in this -- in this quote that I -- this adjudicated fact that I quoted to you, mention is made from the paramilitary formation known as the White Eagles participating in the attack on Foca, and I asked you whether this group was from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: No. I'm sure that the White Eagles were not in Foca at the time. It was the Serb locals who rose to defend their own houses with their own forces. There was no JNA. There was no other military force. It was only the civilian population that rose to defend their houses, to defend their families and villages. As for the White Eagles, nobody mentioned them. Later on there were some military -- paramilitary forces. I don't know what their names were, what the unit's name was, but they were not desirable and welcome in the Serbian Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Vujicic, in paragraph 21 of your statement, you say that the Serbs started to arm only very late, somewhere in mid-1992. And I'm just wondering, are you again mistaken about the year? Would the correct reference, time reference, not be June 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: I only know that the Serbs started arming themselves later. I will admit that. But they started arming themselves much later than the Muslims. The Muslims started doing that. They became the Green Berets and the Mujahedin, and when Focatrans started bringing in weapons, that's where the first depot was. And it was only when the Serbs sensed that there would be an armed conflict in Foca they started arming themselves, and they did it the way they could. There were hunting rifles. There were all sorts of things, and that's how the thing started. It was much later, almost on the eve of the day when the conflict broke out. But I would like to say something else. When it comes to Serbian equipment and weapons, all that would have had a little effect in Foca over those five or six days when Foca was cleansed from the Muslim warriors, but the media helped a lot. There was a journalist in Foca. He was a correspondent --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me stop you here. Let me stop you here, because your written evidence we have already, and we do not need to repeat this. Therefore, I would be very thankful if you would just answer the questions that I ask, because all the other facts are already in -- in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have now another video, and I hope this time it works both with the language -- with the transcript as well, and it's 65 ter 4 -- 40199B. And, Your Honour, as it is being prepared for playing, we have the video and the transcript, and it's an interview of Miroslav Stanic of which the Court has already accepted part as Exhibit P03476, but I would like to play two small bits from this video of Mr. Stanic. And can we please have the first bit played.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] The Serbian Democratic Party at first stopped its political work completely and moved to organise the defence of the Serbian people, the self-defence of the Serbian people, because it has seen the dark clouds rolling towards them. The SDS promptly formed eight battalions which were led, and some of them still are, by the then reserve Serbian first. It worked on the military organisation and the material supplies for the battalions. "I would like to mention something that I never told in public in three, now four years, and that happened in June 1991, during the inspection of that one battalion on the Zlataj mountain when I saw a majestic scene. The battalion was lined up in companies, the quartermaster's unit on the side, and above all of them the tricolour Serbian flag with the cross and the four Ss planted in a hollow beech tree. The Serbs with their national symbols in total illegality on the ground since it was in June 1991 ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sir, Miroslav Stanic, you know that he was the military commander in Foca at the beginning the war; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Miroslav Stanic was president of the municipal organisation of the Serbian Democratic Party. As far as I remember, he was also on the Crisis Staff during the immediate conflict and after. As for this statement he made, I told you that in April, towards the end of April I was mobilised. I was conscripted to our units on the front line. I was inside a bunker facing Gorazde all the way up to June 1994. I have never seen this interview he gave before this day. He might have said this but I cannot say anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But he speaks about eight battalions being formed, and he speaks about this one inspection, and he speaks of June 1991. That would then be correct; right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: If I'm allowed to say this, in June 1991, these units of the Serbian Army, companies, battalions, brigades did not exist. It was all set up much later, in April 1992, once the JNA left Bosnia-Herzegovina. Only then were certain units formed in the municipality of Foca. I know that personally. I know that for a fact, and I stand by it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we now have the next little bit played, and it continues, the interview continues.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] It was strong, and it is a good thing that we prepared in time and that we overestimated is -- overestimated it. And we did not do a song and dance but prepared the military organisation of the Serbian people a year in advance. I have to mention the first wartime commanders, Lazar Kunarac, Zoran Vukovic, Brane Cosovic, Vlado Todovic, Dragan Nikolic, Nade Radovic, Zdravko Kovac, Ljubisa Dostic, Boro Ivanovic, Gojko Jankovic, Pero Elez, Jovan Vukovic, Slavomir Zimanovic called Zuco, and Radmilo Pljevadzic."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sir, as you yourself became a soldier, when the army officially was then formed, the VRS, that is, you know some of these commanders listed here; right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Sorry. All these commanders that he mentioned, that Mr. Stanic mentioned, I know them all only from 1992 and later. I know that from that time on they led certain units. Once the units and the Serbian brigade were formed in Foca, some were battalion commanders, some were commanders of reconnaissance units, of intervention units, that's what I know, and I can say that's how it was. I never heard that they were commanders before that time. Whether they were appointed or not, I did not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Brane Cosovic led which unit to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Some intervention unit, a unit of Brane Cosovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And would that be a unit with the name Dragan Nikolic Unit?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: No. I think Dragan Nikolic was not part of the unit led by Cosovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And -- thank you, sir. Gojko Jankovic led which unit?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Gojko Jankovic also led some reconnaissance unit. It was more of a reconnaissance unit, a unit of scouts that went ahead to see what was going on. When the conflict moved to villages in municipality Foca, when Muslim units raided these villages, then Jankovic's unit was see -- was sent to see how the population, both Muslim and Serb, could be rescued.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. And Mr. Pero Elez --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Pero Elez led the Miljevina Battalion; right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, can this -- can these two excerpts be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Well, we have the same objection to the first -- well, to both of them that we've had before that you overruled. And I think with respect to the first of these clips, there was information that contradicted the witness, and consistent with your ruling, it might be admitted. But on the second clip, I don't think that the witness was contradicted by that and he certainly didn't confirm either of the two clips. So our position is that they both should not be admitted, but if you were to follow your earlier ruling, then only the first clip should be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the second clip is also contradicting the witness because it's the same issue, that is -- that the Serbs -- the Serbs prepared for the war already one year in advance of its start. It's basically the same issue with -- like the first bit. And also the witness confirmed at least the commanders being the right one mentioned here, although he refers to the time period when he was a soldier and there existed the VRS already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: However, given that the relevant part of the transcript were read to the witness and reflected in the transcript, would it be necessary to admit this clip separately?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would rather think it is an important topic here: Who started when -- who prepared and was prepared, and who did it. I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Even if we are to admit this part, it would be admitted only for the credibility issue, wouldn't it? I will consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will also defer ruling this time as well and give it in due course. Please continue, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, I'm aware that I have used up the time you have allocated, but I wish to address a few topics like Partizan Sports Hall and the departure of the Muslims from Foca if you allow me to do this. We had a little bit of problems in the first half hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How much longer would you need, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would think as it is only one more exhibit, basically, I need another 15 minutes perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Vujicic, today and also in paragraph 8 of your statement, you -- you mentioned that Muslims were brought from distant villages where they could not be controlled and protected to certain facilities in Foca where they could be defended, as you call it, and one of these places was Partizan Sports Hall; right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Correct. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You --

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Because Foca -- can I continue? Because Foca was very jagged territory. It was very difficult to cover all houses, be they Muslim or Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sir. Sir, let me stop you. That's already in evidence. We don't need to repeat this. And you --

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes, let's go on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You yourself stood guard there for a few days, and that would be May 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: No, not in May but in April. Between 20th and 24th or 25th of April, 1992. Since I was not mobilised then, I was 55 and under the law they could not mobilise people over 55 --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: -- it was some individuals who --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vujicic, let me cite to you a few facts that this Tribunal established in previous cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Your Honour, I refer here to adjudicated fact 787 from the Krnojelac case and also Kunarac case. "Muslim women were transferred to Buk Bijela, Foca High School, and Partizan Sports Hall. Serb soldiers repeatedly raped Muslim women and girls either at these locations or elsewhere."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sir, as you said this morning that you lived near Partizan, you must have been aware of that, what was going on there, were you not?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: I was there for only three or four nights, only during the night. I don't know what's written there, but I was only there during the night with another guard at the Partizan facility. As for the other premises you mentioned, I have no clue about that. I knew that in the facility I was supposed to guard, some women from the abandoned villages around Foca were placed for their protection. My orders were that nobody must open the doors of that house during the night, and I was even told that I could use force and even shoot if somebody tries.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sir. Sir.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: And that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me stop you. But you're aware that Mr. Kunarac, Mr. Radomir Kovac, and Zoran Vukovic were convicted for assaulting, sexually assaulting women detained in Partizan. Are you not aware of this fact?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: No. In the four days that I was there, nobody got out. I know that women got out only during the day, during daylight nobody -- and they returned at night. After those four days I was mobilised. I don't know what happened later.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Vujicic, in paragraph 8 of your statement and also in paragraphs 31 and 32, you state that Muslim villagers who wanted to stay in their villages were allowed to do so. Mr. Vujicic, before this Court are facts that Muslim villages were attacked and destroyed, and I read to you adjudicated fact 752 from Kunarac. "Once town and villages were securely in the hands, the Serb forces, the military, the police, the paramilitaries, and sometimes even Serb villagers, applied the same pattern. Muslim houses and departments were systematically ransacked or burnt down. Muslim villagers were rounded up or captured and sometimes beaten and killed in the process."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: "Beaten or killed."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: "Beaten or killed." Yes, sorry. I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Vujicic, would you agree that under such conditions Muslims would fear for their lives and try to get out of Foca?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: As for violence, any violence committed by units that launched a counter-offensive against the Muslim units that burnt down Serb villages, because Muslim and Serb villages were close to each other, Serb villages were burnt down and people were killed. I can enumerate several such villages in several areas. However, Serb forces came in and cleansed those areas of those criminals, and the Muslim women and children left or stayed. Those who stayed were mainly women and children and elderly people, and they were admitted into Foca for their own protection. After April, when I was mobilised, we were lined up and the officer read to us instructions how a Serb soldier is supposed to act in cleansing areas from Mujahedins and those criminals. I don't know if anybody was ever hurt except if they were defending themselves or something.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like to have --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I just correct something in line 20? The witness said that the Serb villages were first to be burnt down, including the killing of civilians, and only then did Serbs launch a counter-offensive.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can enumerate those Serb villages in -- in those areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, but that's not necessary. In line 8 on page 79, "down" should read "towns."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have exhibit 65 ter 24393 on the screen. And, Mr. Vujicic, as it is coming up, it is a report of commander Marko Kovac reporting to the Hercegovina Corps command about the situation in Foca on the 10th of October, 1992, and he refers here to a visit of the ICRC from Geneva, and he mentions here that they spoke to certain people, including women and children.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can I please have the English, the second page. The B/C/S is fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sir, if you look at the last sentence here of the report, Kovac states: "If there is interest, we have 21 Muslim children and a number of women for exchange or we would send them to Gorazde." Mr. Vujicic, civilians were used in exchanges, were they not?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were such cases, I know, for a while. This thing that Kovac sent I am seeing for the first time. I was on the front line. I don't know what happened back there. All I know is there have been exchanges of civilians. There was a period when there were exchanges between Foca and Gorazde, all for all. There were also individual exchanges, and some of these people stayed to this day as far as Muslims in Foca are concerned. And there were also exchanges between Foca and Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sir, departure and exchanges, that's not a matter of voluntariness; right? It's not a matter of choice; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: It was their choice and their own freewill. I know that our authorities told them perhaps it's not necessary. At least as far as the population in Foca was concerned. They told them, "Nobody will touch you. You will be safe." And they said, "We have to join our family members who left before the war." I was in the street on one occasion when close friends of mine, Muslims, were talking to me in great detail about these things. They organised their own exchanges, and they went by their own cars and their own buses. Nobody pushed them to do this. Nobody even talked them into it. I know. I know for a fact that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me move to the very last topic I would like to address with you, Mr. Vujicic. In paragraph 22, you refer to Muslim forces fighting from several months, and that this was the reason why the Serb forces attacked the mosques.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can I please have P04070 be brought up on the screen. And can we first have page 130. Your Honour, what is coming up is part of the formatted records of expert Riedlmayer who addressed the destruction of religious sites.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sir, you recognise this mosque, do you?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: I recognise this. This is the Aladza mosque. It seems to me it's the Aladza mosque in Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's correct, sir. Can we now have page 129. Do you recognise this place?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: I can see that some building used to be there, but I can't identify it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That -- the expert that we -- Riedlmayer actually made this photo, and it is the place where the Alaska -- Aladza mosque was actually situated, and that's what it looked like after the war. Sir, the Aladza mosque was destroyed on the 2nd of August, 1992, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: On what date it was destroyed I don't know, but I know that it was blown up. Now, who set the explosives in the mosque and who blew it up, I don't know. All I know, that Muslims stored explosives and weapons in all their mosques because they didn't want it stored in their own family houses. They stored this material in mosques, and from the mosques they defended themselves, and they even trained Green Berets inside mosques. I know about the Pilar mosque in Donje Polje which served exclusively for the training of Muslim extremists.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sir, let me interrupt you. We have all these details. The point is when this mosque, the Aladza mosque, was razed to the ground, there was no fighting from that mosque at that time; right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: No, probably not. Foca at that time was rather quiet. But I want to tell you as far as this mosque and others are concerned, a lot of weaponry, ammunition, and weapons were stored there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sir, let me stop you. Let me stop you here. We have heard that, and this is in evidence. There is no need to repeat this all the time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've -- Your Honour, I forgot that I would like to tender 65 ter 24393.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is the end of my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit P6080. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Several questions. I hope I won't take long.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vujicic, let's begin with the last topic. Has it been established who destroyed the Aladza mosque and whether it could have been hit by a projectile and then destroyed by the explosives stored inside it?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Experts of various nationalities gave it a lot of thought and analysis. It was crazy to put explosives, so many explosives, in that mosque that could have destroyed so many villages around, and it did destroy Muslim and Serb houses in Codor, Mahala, Cerezluk, and the surrounding villages when it exploded. It was a huge amount of explosive, and the detonation was so strong that the area covered was several hundred metres around. Extremists, the conclusion was, put explosives in the mosque that they needed for the combat against Serbs. Now, who blew it up, whether it was a lunatic or an extremist, I don't know. In Cehotina, at the football stadium, you couldn't even see the grass from the debris that came from the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When we are talking about departures, did people leave before the war? Which ethnicity left Foca before the war?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Everybody, Serbs, Muslims, everybody. For example, in my building where there were 40 apartments, everybody left. Only my neighbour and myself remained in the building. In my building, there are five Muslims and five Serbs. They all left save for me. I did not have anywhere to go. When things calmed down a little in Foca, Serbs returned, even Muslims did. I know a family from Koplje [as interpreted]. A woman was married to a guy in Uskoplje and her husband and herself and her sister remained in Foca. They tried to take her out with them to Foca when they crossed Stjepan Polje, and they proceeded across the rivers of the Drina and Sutjeska. Muslim forces came across the river. They ambushed them and they killed them. In that family there were two more men of Serb ethnicities who were also on the way to Foca. They were also killed. There were many Muslim families that left Foca individually after having lived in the area for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the attitude of Muslim extremists towards those Muslims who lived normally with Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Well, there were no favours. There were no love lost between them. I don't know whether anybody was killed or not, but it was held against them. But to be honest, in Foca there were Serbs and Muslims who believed that all those tensions had to be diminished and that it had to be made sure that nothing arrived at Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the name of Halid Cengic? What can you tell us about his activities?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: I know Halid Cengic well. He was from a noble family --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That was not raised in the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it was. While there were preparations for the war. This is my foundation for the questions that I'm going to put later on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please tell us first how -- or from where this question arose.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From a claim by Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff that the Serbs were the first who started preparing themselves for the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think she led evidence to at that effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, I never claimed that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, it was said that the war started in 1991. I want to establish when Halid Cengic started preparing Muslims for the war, and every Serb in Foca knows that only too well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please move on to your next topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. With respect to this issue, the Prosecution attempted to show that the Serbs were preparing for war well before the war broke out in Foca, and it doesn't -- it seems like Dr. Karadzic should have the opportunity to show what -- what circumstances were taking place during that time, and particularly what the other side was doing. It's not tu quoque evidence. It's related to the topic that -- the point that Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff was trying to make, which was the Serbs were preparing. And if -- we can't have a trial here where you can only show that one side is preparing for war and then don't hear evidence that the other side, what they were doing. So I think that it's within her cross-examination, and it's very relevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Would you like to add anything?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. This witness has -- has in his written evidence the claim that the Muslims prepared for war. They had the Green Berets and they were armed and they had their weapons in the mosque, they had their explosives in the mosque. And also in the evidence we have from the witness in writing and also here, we -- this morning that the Serbs did not do that. On the contrary, they only started to arm themselves when the conflict started, and in his written evidence he even speaks of June 1992. And all I did in the cross-examination, show him that this is not correct, at least not to -- according to what Mr. Stanic said and according to the evidence that is in front of this Court. I did not say anything more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: But, Mr. President, that opens the door to Dr. Karadzic to be able to ask what the Muslims were doing and whether what the Serbs were doing was in response to that or creating some situation in Foca unilaterally. So I think that topic is fair game for redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, the Chamber agrees with Mr. Robinson's observation, the last one. The Chamber will allow the accused to put that question. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujicic, can you tell us, when did the Muslims started organising themselves and who was it who started organising them?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: I've already said that the Muslims started arming themselves from 1989 through Focatrans and in many other ways. The Serbs started doing that much later. I don't know whether it was before 1991. In any case, both ethnicities armed themselves, but Serbs started doing that much later than the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As far as Focatrans is concerned, I'm not going to tell you about the Serb rights -- being deprived of their rights, but when it comes to arming, why did you mention Focatrans? How did arming take place through Focatrans?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Focatrans was an operation in miniature, as an experiment as to how the Serbs were going to react at the time when Bosnia and Herzegovina was proclaimed as an independent state of Muslims, and in terms of those declarations and proclamations and articles in newspapers, whatever happened in Focatrans was later on reconfirmed by the events. First of all, Serbs were fired and Muslims were hired, and then they started removing Serb drivers from lorries and buses, and they appointed Muslims in their place and so on and so forth. I would like to tell you something, Mr. Karadzic. I would like to tell you this: In Foca there was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Vujicic, I think you answered the question. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujicic, what was the attitude of the civilian authorities towards departures; i.e., did you know that the civilian authorities placed a ban on the departure of Serbs and Muslims at first and that ban was lifted later on?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether there was a ban, but I know that it was always said there was no need for anybody to leave Foca. I know that personally. I heard announcements. And every individual who came to various municipal departments of the Serbian authorities, that's what they were told. Some people stayed -- stayed behind. They stayed in Foca throughout the war. They didn't come in harm's way. They are still there. They can testify to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber saw a document banning departure. I cannot quote it. When I find it, I will. It has been admitted into evidence. But let me ask you this, you are an educated man. You occupied different positions in different companies: Is it correct -- or, rather, in the Law on All People's Defence, is it prescribed that the ruling party should organise All People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: These are leading questions now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question was about organising battalions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I was going to ask who was it who had the right to have a Territorial Defence unit in the former system?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Before the war, the Territorial Defence was organised by Foca municipality. It had its own Territorial Defence. It had its equipment for manoeuvres and so on and so forth. When the war broke out, everything fell apart. The territorial depot had some weapons, but that was seized by somebody, but all that happened later. So whatever used to belong to Yugoslavia, everything fell apart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the issue of Territorial Defence was not discussed with the witness and the structures in the municipality of -- to this effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I agree, but you rose after the witness had already answered the question. Shall we conclude --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, there were eight battalions mentioned here. I'm asking the witness whether the companies or anybody else had the right to form Territorial Defence units apart from the municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. When the war broke out, people rose spontaneously in order to defend their houses, their villages, and their families, and the battalions of the so-called Army of Republika Srpska, when the JNA withdrew, brigades started being set up on both sides. For example, there was the Muslim brigade known as the Sutjeska Brigade which was present in the territory of Foca municipality until August. They stormed the Serbian villages and set them on fire. And then the Serbian people organised themselves and chased those Muslims to Trnovo. For a long time that brigade was active in Trnovo. The so-called Sutjeska Brigade of Foca as it was known. And the Serbs -- I apologise. The Serbs --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the end of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, you were read --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You spoke a little too fast. The interpreters couldn't hear you, in particular the last part. After you said, "I apologise," what did you say, Mr. Vujicic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the Serbs and the Sutjeska in one sentence. Do you hear me, Mr. Vujicic?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Your answer was not recorded completely. You said, "I apologise, but the Serbs occupied the Sutjeska. You did not hear that. I heard it -- what did you say about the Sutjeska and the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: When the Muslim unit known as the Sutjeska brigade, which was active in the territory of Tjentiste until September 1992, it stormed Serbian villages and torched them and some individual houses between the Muslim villages, all of those were burned. Fortunately enough, there were no civilians because they had left the area beforehand. And then the Serbian forces set out and chased those Muslim warriors, and they moved to the territory of Trnovo. I don't know whether I have told you enough. I can go on, but this is all I know. In this month of September 1992, when the JNA left that area of the Sutjeska, there was the 4th Battalion of the Foca Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Two adjudicated facts were read out to you earlier today, inter alia, that fire was opened from Kalinovik on Foca. How far is Kalinovik from Foca? What is the terrain between Foca and Kalinovik? Could one open fire from Kalinovik on Foca?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: No, not in Kalinovik. I don't know whether there was the kind of activity that could open fire from Kalinovik on Foca. Between the two there is a mountain over 1.100 metres old and then there is Miljevina and another hilltop, and only then could a shell have reached Foca. I don't know if there is that kind of artillery, perhaps Verder or something else that could hit Foca from Kalinovik. There were military barracks of the former JNA there. The Serbian Army of the Republika Srpska did not have that kind of weaponry. They didn't open fire. Even if the JNA had opened fire from Kalinovik, it -- Foca was out of its range. Do you know how far that is? It is over 40 kilometres from Kalinovik to Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So that adjudicated fact is not correct, is it?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: No, it's not. I energetically refute that. I deny it, I'm sure, and I apply my public statement to that with my head raised high. Let the whole world watch me when I say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Another adjudicated fact was read out to you according to which when Serbs took Muslim villages and towns they would torch them and they would kill people. What is your opinion of that adjudicated fact when it comes to Foca and the villages and settlements around Foca?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: I must say that when I was mobilised on Easter, on the 26th of April, 1992, we were lined up, and we were read an order, a written order, as to how a Serbian soldier had to behave, and the gist of that was to chase warriors who had persecuted people in the Serbian villages. There was nothing to the effect that houses had to be torched, that civilians had to be killed. It was just the contrary, that the civilians had to be protected and that they should be received in reception centres in Foca if no other solution was at hand. Some sort of the Geneva Conventions were read out regarding wartime behaviour, but I'd known them from before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I don't have the time to read Mr. Stanic's answer where he says that Muslim formations were strong and the Serbs did not underestimate them. I don't have the time, so I'll give up on that. Mr. Vujicic, thank you very much for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Not at all.
